entries.text: Hi there — I'm Sarah, an AI researcher with HeliumDeploy. Thank you so much for taking 15 minutes to do this — it really means a lot. Honestly, the more you can share with me, the better — we're aiming for about a thousand words of feedback together, so please don't worry about going long. The founders read every word of these chats, so what you say actually shapes what HD does next. As a thank-you you'll get a $75 discount code at the end. So — to kick us off, what brought you to HD recently?
Looking for good deals on minors? Trying to get the best bang for the buck. Easy setup, and quick response. That's pretty much it.

Got it — best bang for the buck, easy setup, quick response. Let me pull up the one you spent the most time on. You looked at the NerdQaxe a couple of times the other night — what did you think of it?

See, nerd. Quad is six point one six terabyte terahash per second. Was very interesting. However, I was kinda confused how it's using the ASIC chip thirteen seventy and pulling that much hash rate from that chip versus the Okta. With, uh, it only pulls in, like, nine point six terahash. So I was kinda confused if they were running it hot so it could deliver or were they run it fairly relaxed and still produce that kinda terahash
That's a sharp observation — same BM1370 silicon, very different output per chip. Did you go digging anywhere specific to figure that out — Reddit, the manufacturer's spec sheet, somewhere else?
Uh, the specs came from the Helium Deploy website. Is where I picked up on it.

Got it — so you were comparing the two product pages side by side here on HD. Let me bring up the Octaxe too. When you saw the NerdQaxe pulling 6 TH/s from one chip and the Octaxe averaging 1.2 per chip — what did that make you think? Like, did one feel like the safer buy or the riskier buy?

I question the error rate and I was wondering how accurate it was gonna be by overclocking to try to hit twelve terahash that was being projected that could hit instead of its nine point eight or nine point six terahash a second. It running at cooler and less energy. Was not sure if that's gonna cause a higher uh, failure rate or not versus the smaller machine at six terahash. That possibly be more efficient And does it being Wi Fi have any bearing on any of this at all?

Really interesting — so you're weighing reliability against the headline hashrate, not just chasing the biggest number. Why does failure rate weigh on you so heavily? Have you had a miner die on you before?

All minors have been left at the optimum settings for cooling and power efficiency. And so far, none of them have failed. Thus far, it runs pretty smooth, but as I said to begin with, it's about getting the most terahash for the power and then bang for the buck.
Okay, that lands — you keep them stock, no overclocking, and so far zero failures. So when you say bang for the buck, what miners do you already have running today?
Prefer not just go into that this time.
No problem at all, totally respect that. Let's stay on what you were shopping. You also pulled up the NEXUS L1 — that's a different beast, an altcoin miner. What pulled you over to that one?

I've only done Bitcoin mining thus far or ASIC mining rather. Uh, have not done any script mining. Was thinking about diversifying and breaking off and looking into that a little bit. And this point in time, I have none. But, uh, am kinda interested in it. This is totally for a hobby for me, not for profit. And just for fun. So because of that, the bottom line is very important to keep a close eye on

That's a great frame — hobby, not profit, so the bottom line matters even more because nothing's subsidizing the losses. Why scrypt though? What got you curious about diversifying off SHA-256 specifically?

Just something different that I don't know much about. I like learning new things. And there's no research I've done on my side, really, to show that that would be a good idea or a bad idea at this point. Right now, just keep everything focusing in house, running on my own Bitnode. So that's kinda where I'm at.

Got it — running your own Bitcoin node, mining at home, and now curious about scrypt purely as a learning exercise. That's a great picture.

Let me jump back to the NerdQaxe for a second — you said bang for the buck matters most. Let me show you something. NerdQaxe is $249 for 6 TH/s — that's about $41 per terahash. The Avalon Q here is $1,700 for 90 TH/s — about $19 per terahash. Less than half the cost per hash. Have you looked at this one?
No. I have not.

Take a quick look — it's a 90 TH/s home miner, pulls about 3.5 kW, runs around 50 dB so it's quiet for that scale. On paper it's the best $/TH in HD's lineup by a wide margin. What's your gut reaction looking at it?
First question comes to mind's power consumption. Need to run some conversion numbers on it. Second is how affordable or how soon it's available Uh, according to this here, it says it's out of stock.

Good catch — yeah, it's currently out of stock. So power consumption is the first thing your brain jumps to. Tell me about that — what's your electricity situation at home, and what's the ceiling you won't cross?

Currently, I got a good rate at point nine cents per kilowatt. So I don't have a lot of pressure there. But at some point, I would like to push this more towards a subsidized power distribution based off of solar panels I have not started on that at all at this point in time. However, the ninety terahash is very appealing.

Wow, 9 cents/kWh and you're already thinking about solar to subsidize further — you're playing the long game. So at 9 cents, even a 3.5 kW Avalon Q only costs you about $7.50 a day to run. That's not the wall. What is the wall, then — is it the $1,700 upfront, or something else holding you back from a machine like that?
Uh, pretty much the total price is, uh, not in my scope of things to be able to do at this point in time. And currently, it shows to be fifteen hundred dollars. Is that correct?

Let me point you at the right number. It's listed at $1,700. So the upfront cap····the real wall — makes total sense. When you think about your hobby budget for a single miner, what's the number that feels comfortable versus the number that feels like a stretch?
Uh, usually two fifty to throw it at every couple months. Stretch is usually why I hit the six, seven hundred dollar mark. In that same time frame.

Perfect — that explains exactly why the NerdQaxe at $249 was your sweet spot, and the Octaxe at $469 was the stretch you were weighing. That's really clear now.

One more thing I'm curious about — when you're researching a miner before you buy, where do you go besides HD's site? Like the other night when you were comparing the NerdQaxe and Octaxe specs, did you cross-check anywhere else?

There is two other companies that I've compare it to. Uh, not really sure. They all look the same to me. As far as specs go. The, uh, sales is what I try to be on the lookout for. And that's usually where I'll go where I'll go where I can make the best deal with the most reliable customer service in case there's problems.
That's gold — reliable customer service in case there's problems. Have you ever had to actually use customer service on a miner purchase — a return, a defective unit, anything like that?
Not as of yet. Everything has been well packaged and worked. Seamlessly. Right out of the box. The setup time was very minimum.

Nice — clean track record so far. So when you say you pick the vendor with the most reliable customer service "in case" — you're buying insurance you've never had to cash in. Where does that confidence come from for a given vendor? Like how do you actually judge that before you buy?
Based on user's comments and other forums, and who report their personal interactions
Got it — so other buyers' stories on forums are doing the heavy lifting. Which forums or communities are you actually reading? Reddit, Discord, YouTube comments, somewhere else?
All three.
All three — perfect. Any specific subreddit or Discord or YouTube channel you trust more than the others when you're vetting a vendor?

Not really. I just kinda mosey through all of them and make notes of the negative comments that come from. Different users Some of the, uh, YouTube users I follow don't represent any particular company. Those I tend to value a little bit heavier than those who are pushing to offer a significant discount. Uh, by hyping one up over another.

That makes total sense — independent voices over the discount-code affiliates. Smart filter.

Last thread before we wrap — when you've been moseying through Reddit and YouTube comments lately, has anything negative about HD specifically come up? Or has it been clean?
Thus far, I've not discovered any negative yet.

That's really good to hear, and honestly really useful signal for us.

Okay — this has been incredibly helpful, Scott. Just to play back what I heard: hobby miner, not chasing profit, $250 sweet spot with $600-700 as a stretch, very technical brain that digs into chip specs and failure rates, 9-cent power with solar on the horizon, and you vet vendors through independent voices on Reddit, Discord, and YouTube before you ever click buy. The N. question was really about whether the bigger one is being pushed too hard on the same silicon — that's a sharp question we should probably answer better on the product page.

Before we close — is there anything we didn't cover that you wish we had?

Why not make a unit like the ninety terahash unit you were showing me but it has like, forty five terahash. Would be my only recommendation. It's a pretty big jump. From the ten terahash up to ninety terahash leaving a gaping hole in the middle.

That is a fantastic piece of product feedback — a 40-something TH/s middle tier between the Octaxe and the Avalon Q, probably in the $700-900 range, which would land right in your stretch budget. I'm writing that one down in bold for the founders. There's a real gap there.

Thank you so much, Scott — this was genuinely one of the more thoughtful conversations I've had. Your $75 discount code will land in your inbox at (email hidden) shortly. Have a great day.
Thank you.
Take care.
